readme: # Replication Package: How Developers Experience Debugging Unfamiliar Codebases with Code Tours Generated and Evaluated by Local LLMs [REDACTED] [REDACTED] This repository contains the code, data, and instructions needed to replicate the experiments described in the paper. Each step is documented with its full parameters, expected outputs, and archived intermediate results: so you can either run the entire pipeline end-to-end or jump in at any stage using our pre-computed data. If you only want a quick end-to-end check, we provide a **minimal example** that reproduces a single code tour from the paper (Code Tour 32; Figure 10; mwilliamson-java-mammoth, commit [`b65bc06`](https://github.com/mwilliamson/java-mammoth/commit/b65bc063d98c2ddb1dc4cc9b4dbcdc1aef23d5aa)). Look for the **Minimal example** blocks throughout. > ⚠️ **Before you start**: download the data archive from Zenodo and extract it into [`./data`](./data) (~50 GB of tar files). These archives contain the intermediate results of each pipeline stage, letting you skip expensive steps. ## Pipeline overview | Stage | Input | Output | Count | |---|---|---|---| | [1. Collect bug-fixes](#1--collecting-reproducible-bug-fixes) | GitHub repos | Non-flaky reproducible bug-fixes | 110 across 30 projects | | [2. Collect stack traces](#2--collecting-stack-traces) | Bug-fixes | Stack traces → sampled subset | 243 across 15 projects | | [3. Generate code tours](#3--generating-code-tours) | Sampled stack traces | Code tours | 26 | | [4. Evaluate code tours](#4--evaluating-code-tours) | Code tours | Annotations | 52 | | [5. Evaluate with developers](#5--evaluation-with-developers) | Code tours+Annotations | Codebook | — | ## Prerequisites ### Software * [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) (29.5.1 or later) * [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) (v5.1.3 or later) * Gitbug-Actions and Gitbug-Java (see [Section 1](#1--collecting-reproducible-bug-fixes) and [Section 2.1](#21--setting-the-gitbug-java-cli)) * [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) (v0.30.9 or later); we ran it on-prem. * (Optional) [Poetry](https://python-poetry.org/) (v2.0.1 or later) for running Python scripts outside Docker * (Optional) [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/) for exposing the web interface to external participants ### Hardware * **Disk:** more than 50 GB of free space for the data archives and intermediate results. ⚠️ The dockers from gitbug's pipeline can eat a lot of disk space. * **RAM (for LLM)** depends on the model you want to run of course but Devstral Small 1.1 (used in the study) required ~15 GB of RAM. * **Runtime expectations**: Stage 1 is the bottleneck and can take days or weeks. Stage 2 can take hours. Stages 3 and 4 the bottleneck is the LLM inference time. Stage 5 developers usually took around 10 minutes to discuss a tour. ### Conventions used in this document * 📅 highlights parameters tied to dates so you can see which one to adjust to evaluate newer models and prevent data leakage * 📥 / 📤 mark input / output paths * ⚙️ reports the result counts from our runs * 📦 points to the archived data for skipping a step ## 1 — Collecting reproducible bug-fixes We use [Gitbug-Actions](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions) to collect reproducible bug fixes. See its [README](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions#readme) for installation. We vendor the legacy version used in this study under `code/gitbugactions`, but cloning a newer version is recommended for new studies. > 📅 **Data leakage:** to evaluate recent models, collect bug fixes from *after* the model's training cutoff. The study window was 2025. ### 1.1 — Collecting repositories **Repositories** were collected with [`collect_repos.py`](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions/blob/main/collect_repos.py), using the following GitHub search parameters: * `--query ...` — the search query to find repositories: * `language:Java` — Java repositories * `stars:>20` — more than 20 stars * `archived:false` — not archived * `pushed:2025-01-01..2025-12-31` — pushed during 2025 📅 * `--out_path ./out/gitbugs/repos` — output path for the repositories 📤 > ⚙️ Run: > ```bash > cd code/gitbugactions > python collect_repos.py \ > --query "language:Java stars:>20 archived:false pushed:2025-01-01..2025-12-31" \ > --out_path ./out/gitbugs/repos > ``` > > Resulted in **11,495** repos screened with **17,284** commits analysed. > 📦 Skip this step: extract the archived [`repos`](data/repos.tar) and [`commits`](data/commits.tar.gz): > > ```bash > mkdir -p ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/{repos,commits} > tar -xvf data/repos.tar -C ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/repos > tar -xvf data/commits.tar.gz -C ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/commits > ``` > ⚠️ Star counts (and other parameters) may change over time, so re-running this query today may return different repositories than the original study. ### 1.2 — Identifying bug-fix commits **Bug-fix commits** — *commits with passing tests after the commit* — were identified with the [`collect_bugs.py`](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions/blob/main/collect_bugs.py), with the following parameters: * `--n_workers 5` — use 5 workers * `--filter_on_commit_message False` — keep all commits (i.e., do **not** filter by "fix" keyword) * `--filter_on_commit_time_start "2025-01-01 00:00 UTC" --filter_on_commit_time_end "2026-01-01 00:00 UTC"` — restrict to 2025 📅 * `--strategies PASS_PASS, FAIL_PASS` — keep commits with passing tests after the commit * `--data_path ./out/gitbugs/repos` — path to the folder containing the repositories 📥 * `--commit_list_file ...` — path to a JSON file containing a list of commit URLs to analyze. We paginate (11 pages) to circumvent API limitations in [`commits`](data/commits.tar.gz) 📥 * `--results_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs` — folder on which the results will be saved. 📤 > ⚙️ **Run:** > ```bash > cd code/gitbugactions > python collect_bugs.py \ > --n_workers 5 \ > --filter_on_commit_message False \ > --filter_on_commit_time_start "2025-01-01 00:00 UTC" \ > --filter_on_commit_time_end "2026-01-01 00:00 UTC" \ > --strategies PASS_PASS, FAIL_PASS \ > --data_path ./out/gitbugs/repos \ > --commit_list_file ./out/gitbugs/commits/commits.json \ > --results_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs > ``` > > **Result:** **162** bug-fix commits. > 📦 Skip this step: extract [`gitbugs.tar.gz`](data/gitbugs.tar.gz): > > ```bash > mkdir -p ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/bugs > tar -xvf data/gitbugs.tar.gz -C ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/bugs >``` ### 1.3 — Exporting and filtering bug-fix commits Each bug fix is **dockerized** with [`export_bugs.py`](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions/blob/main/export_bugs.py). * `--dataset_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs/` — path where the results of collect_bugs are stored 📥 * `--output_folder_path ./out/gitbugs/export/` — folder on which the results will be saved 📤 ```bash cd code/gitbugactions python export_bugs.py \ --dataset_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs/ \ --output_folder_path ./out/gitbugs/export/ ``` Commits that are **flaky** — *across multiple runs, the tests do not always pass* — are filtered out with [`filter_bugs.py`](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbugactions/blob/main/filter_bugs.py) and the following parameters: * `--n_workers 5` — use 5 workers * `--bugs_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs/` — path to the results from [Step 1.2](#12--identifying-bug-fix-commits) 📥 * `--export_path ./out/gitbugs/export/` — path to the results from [Step 1.3](#13--exporting-and-filtering-bug-fix-commits) 📥 * `--res_path ./out/gitbugs/res/` — folder on which the results will be saved 📤 ```bash cd code/gitbugactions python filter_bugs.py \ --n_workers 5 \ --bugs_path ./out/gitbugs/bugs/ \ --export_path ./out/gitbugs/export/ \ --res_path ./out/gitbugs/res/ ``` > ⚙️ Resulted in **110** non-flaky, offline reproducible bug fixes across **30** projects. > 📦 Archived in tar file [`gitbugs/export`](data/gitbugs.tar.gz) and [`gitbugs/res`](data/gitbugs.tar.gz). ```bash mkdir -p ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/export mkdir -p ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/res tar -xvf data/gitbugs.tar.gz -C ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/export tar -xvf data/gitbugs.tar.gz -C ./code/gitbugactions/out/gitbugs/res ``` ## 2 — Collecting stack traces ### 2.1 — Setting the gitbug-java CLI The [Gitbug-Java](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbug-java) project provides a command line interface (CLI) that allows you to interact with Java reproducible bugs collected with gitbug-actions. It is used in the pipeline to collect stack traces. The tar file [`gitbugs`](data/gitbugs.tar.gz) contains the reproducible bug fixes in a format that can be used directly with the [Gitbug-Java CLI](https://github.com/gitbugactions/gitbug-java). ```bash tar -xvf data/gitbugs.tar.gz -C ./code/gitbug-java ``` ### 2.2 — Setting environment The `CodeTourGen` project can be run directly inside Docker. To build the container and start the script runner, run: ```bash cd code/CodeTourGen docker compose build docker compose up -d ``` Then you can exectute scripts inside the container with: ```bash docker compose exec codetourgen bash ``` ### 2.3 — Collecting stack traces **Stack traces** are collected by running the [`generate_stacktrace.py`](code/CodeTourGen/generate_stacktrace.py) script with the following parameters: * `--benchmark gitbugs` — uses the Gitbug-Java CLI to interact with reproducible bugs (see [Section 2.1](#21--setting-the-gitbug-java-cli)) * `--extractor treesitter` — extracts code snippets using [Tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/) instead of [CodeQL](https://codeql.github.com/) ```bash cd code/CodeTourGen docker compose exec codetourgen bash python generate_stacktrace.py \ --benchmark gitbugs \ --extractor treesitter ``` > ⚙️ Resulted in **243** stack traces across **15** projects. **Minimal working example:** ```bash cd code/CodeTourGen docker compose exec codetourgen bash poetry run python generate_stacktrace.py \ --benchmark gitbugs \ --extractor treesitter \ --version b65bc063d98c \ --project mwilliamson-java-mammoth ``` > 📦 Archived in tar file [`stacktraces`](data/stacktraces.tar.gz). ```bash mkdir -p ./code/CodeTourGen/data/stacktraces tar -xvf data/stacktraces.tar.gz -C ./code/CodeTourGen/data/stacktraces ``` ### 2.4 — Sampling stack traces For code tour generation ([Section 3](#3--generating-code-tours)), we sample a subset of the 243 stack traces, **randomly stratified per project and error type**, using the [`sampling_rounds.py`](code/CodeTourGen/scripts/sampling_rounds.py) script with the following parameters: * `--input data/tour_records.csv` — CSV with the collected stack trace records 📥 * `--rounds 2` — two sampling rounds * `--nb-samples-per-round 1,1` — one sample per project/error pair per round * `--total-per-round 13` — 13 stack traces selected per round * `--random-state 2026` — fixed seed for reproducibility * `--output-dir data/samples_round` — output directory for the sampled traces 📤 ```bash cd code/CodeTourGen docker compose exec codetourgen bash poetry run python scripts/sampling_rounds.py \ --input data/tour_records.csv \ --rounds 2 \ --nb-samples-per-round 1,1 \ --total-per-round 13 \ --random-state 2026 \ --output-dir data/samples_round ``` > ⚙️ Resulted in **26** sampled stack traces (2 rounds × 13). > 📦 The [`data/samples_round`](data/samples_round/) folder contains the sampled traces for each round. ![](./figures/samples.png) ```bash mkdir -p ./code/CodeTourGen/data/samples_round tar -xvf data/samples_round.tar.gz -C ./code/CodeTourGen/data/samples_round ``` ## 3 — Generating code tours ### 3.1 — Setting the ollama instance > For both the code tour generation and evaluation, we use an ollama instance that runs on a on-prem server. See [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) for installation instructions. You need to add in the `.env` file the following environment variables: ```.env OLLAMA_HOST=... ``` In the study, we used the following model: * [Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B](https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5-coder:14b/blobs/ac9bc7a69dab) * [DeepSeek Coder v2 16B](https://ollama.com/library/deepseek-coder-v2:16b/blobs/5ff0abeeac1d) * [Devstral Small 1.1](https://ollama.com/SimonPu/Devstral-Small:2507-Q4_K_XL/blobs/f352346d3b64) ### 3.2 — Generating code tours **Code tours** are **generated** by running the [`generate_codetour.py`](code/CodeTourGen/generate_codetour.py) script, with those parameters: * `--strategy whole` — generate the whole code tour in one step. * `--temperature 1 --top_p 1` — use a temperature of 1 and a top-p of 1 for the LLM. > 💻 The shell script [`generate_codetour.sh`](cmd/generate_codetour.sh) replicates the runs of the code tour generation for each of the 26 sampled stack traces. > ⚙️ Resulted in **26** code tours across **15** projects. **Minimal example:** ```bash cd code/CodeTourGen docker compose exec codetourgen bash poetry run python generate_codetour.py --generator qwen2.5-coder:14b --project mwilliamson-java-mammoth --version b65bc063d98c --tour 3 ``` > 📦 Archived in tar file [`codetours`](data/codetours.tar.gz). ```bash mkdir -p ./code/CodeTourGen/data/codetours tar -xvf data/codetours.tar.gz -C ./code/CodeTourGen/data/codetours ``` ## 4 — Evaluating code tours **Code tours** are **evaluated** by running the [`eval_codetour.py`](code/CodeTourGen/eval_codetour.py) script, with those parameters: * `--max_tokens 100` — use a maximum of 100 tokens for the LLM. > 💻 The shell script [`eval_codetour.sh`](cmd/eval_codetour.sh) replicates the runs of the two evaluation configurations for the code tour evaluation for each code tour generated. > ⚙️ This resulted in **52** evaluations, 2 per code tour. > 📦 Archived in tar file [`evals`](data/evals.tar.gz). ```bash mkdir -p ./code/CodeTourEval/data/evals tar -xvf data/evals.tar.gz -C ./code/CodeTourEval/data/evals ``` **Minimal Example:** ```bash cd code/CodeTourEval docker compose exec codetoureval bash poetry run python eval_codetour.py --bid 42 --judge deepseek-coder-v2:16b --project mwilliamson-java-mammoth --version b65bc063d98c --tour 3 ``` ## 5 — Evaluation with developers This section describes how to run the web application we used to conduct the evaluation study with developers and also to explore the data collected during the study. ### 5.1 — Starting the web interface The web interface is a Flask application that runs inside a Docker container. To start it, run: ```bash cd code/CodeTourEvalWeb mkdir -p data docker compose build docker compose up -d ``` > ⚠️ You need to setup the following environment variables in a `.env` file (we use the dummy values `codetoureval` for all): ```.env DB_USER=... DB_PASSWORD=... DB_NAME=... ``` Once the containers are up, the web interface is available locally at http://localhost:5000. > 💡 We used [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/) to expose the web interface only when we were running an interview and participants could use their own computers. ### 5.2 — Loading the replication data To explore the data from the study, you need to (1) extract the data and (2) import it to the database ([PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/)). **Step 1 — Extracting the study files.** Extract [`eval-data.tar.gz`](data/eval-data.tar.gz) into the [`./data`](./data) folder of [CodeTourEvalWeb](code/CodeTourEvalWeb/): ```bash mkdir -p ./code/CodeTourEvalWeb/data tar -xvf data/eval-data.tar.gz -C code/CodeTourEvalWeb/data cp data/database_dump.sql ./code/CodeTourEvalWeb/ ``` **Step 2 — Importing the database.** Load the database dump ([`database_dump.sql`](data/database_dump.sql)) into the [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) database used by the web interface: ```bash cd code/CodeTourEvalWeb docker compose exec db psql -U codetoureval -d codetoureval -c "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;" docker compose exec -T db psql -U codetoureval -d codetoureval < database_dump.sql docker compose up -d ``` ### 5.3 — Routes The application has three main pages: **Home — `/`** The entry point: participants can read the instructions and click **Start Evaluation** to begin the evaluation. ![](./figures/home.png) This takes them to a form where they enter their information (Java Level, Dev experience and degree). ![](./figures/form.png) After submitting, they are presented with the code tours assigned to them and the corresponding judgement annotations. ![](./figures/assignment.png) **Review — `/review//`** A **read-only** view of a participant's completed evaluation. Use the navigation panel on the left to switch between participants and their assigned tours. For each tour, this page shows: * the code tour as the participant saw it, * the ratings the participant gave to each annotation, and * the comments the participant left about the tour. ![](./figures/review_1.png) ---- ![](./figures/review_2.png) **Codebook — `/codebook`** Displays the codebook used in our qualitative analysis. **Step 1 to 5** show the evolution of the inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) at each coding round, with codes split into three sections according to their agreement level: **strong** ($\alpha > 0.8$), **tentative** ($0.66 < \alpha < 0.8$), and **unreliable** ($\alpha < 0.66$). ![](./figures/codebook_rounds.png) **Final step** shows the final codebook used in the analysis. Each code is presented with: * the external ID used in the paper, * its decomposition into valence, component, property, and goal, and * the number of participants who expressed the experience at least once (hover over the count to see the list of participants). ![](./figures/codebook_final.png)
